doc.title: Onaje Allan Gumbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Where the new jazz standards are
summary: He complains that players recycle old standards and new jazz rarely produces singable tunes.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I’ve often wondered that. Where are they going to come from?

You know, we’re still doing “Stella By Starlight” and you know, all these tunes, as great as they are, whether it’s “I Remember Clifford” or whatever, the reason they wrote these tunes, Benny wrote “I Remember Clifford” — he didn’t want to play what was done thirty years before that. You know. And it’s good to have in the repertoire, but understanding the momentum, you know, in other music people are constantly writing new songs, in country & western music and everybody’s constantly writing new tunes. And new tunes that people can sing, they can really listen to. Somehow jazz takes again this classical approach. Like how many times are you going to do Beethoven’s Ninth? How many times are you going to Carmina Burana? How many times are you going to do Puccini aria from whatever? Okay? And the new music is usually an exercise in how many notes can I get in between two measures? How slick can I make the chord progression? And one thing that bothers me is the lack of engagement of the audience. Because one of the things that jazz does not share with the other more popular music of the day, mainly rap, R&B, pop, whatever, is that audience participation is part and parcel of the presentation. It’s what makes the whole presentation come alive, is actually the response of the audience to the music. In jazz it’s about a quiet policy, and a polite applause between solos. You see? And that’s it. And okay we don’t have a problem with that. But short of that, can’t you at least talk to the audience? Can’t you like let them know what you’re playing? Or maybe who wrote it? You see? It doesn’t happen.
